extracted.intended_audience: aspiring screenwriters, screenwriters, and filmmakers interested in story craft
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, high-level and scene-level guidelines for designing and writing cinematic stories and screenplays (structure, character, scene, dialogue, image systems, pacing, and problem-solving).

rubrics_metrics.name: Story: principles not rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is about principles not rules; eternal, universal forms not formulas; archetypes not stereotypes; thoroughness not shortcuts; realities, not mysteries; mastering the art, not second-guessing the marketplace; respect for the audience; originality not duplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor deep, durable principles over prescriptive formulas. Strive for originality, respect the audience, avoid shortcuts and stereotyping; focus on mastering craft rather than chasing trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beats → Scenes → Sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Beats build scenes, scenes build sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design stories from the smallest dramatic units (beats) upward; ensure each beat contributes to scene purpose and each scene to sequence/act objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story values (value at stake)
rubrics_metrics.description: Story values are universal human qualities that may shift from positive to negative or vice versa through conflict; ask of each scene: what value is at stake in my character’s life right now?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify opening and closing value for scenes; if a scene's value doesn't change, it's a nonevent. Use value swings to dramatize meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical Design / Archplot requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Archplot — story built around an active protagonist who struggles against primarily external forces to pursue desire through continuous time within a consistent, causally connected reality, leading to a closed ending of absolute irreversible change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key features: causality, closed ending, linear time, external conflict, single active protagonist, consistent reality. Use as a template when aiming for classical Hollywood storytelling; examples given (Seven Samurai, 2001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimalism / Miniplot features
rubrics_metrics.description: Miniplot — open ending, internal conflict, multi-protagonists, passive protagonist; less various than Archplot, mostly international examples (Tender Mercies, Wild Strawberries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for quieter, character-internal tales where closure and external action are minimized; expect a different audience expectation set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-Structure / Antiplot features
rubrics_metrics.description: Antiplot — coincidence, nonlinear time, inconsistent realities; predominately European post‑WWII (8½, Persona).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antiplot intentionally substitutes coincidence or nonlinearity for causality; use deliberately and consistently if choosing this form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality over coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Causality — interconnectedness of reality; a story must obey its own internal laws of probability. Coincidence is the disconnectedness of existence and is an enemy of meaningful story unless dramatized to gain meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reliance on coincidence to solve plot problems (especially late). If you use coincidence, introduce it early and let it gain meaning; never use coincidence to turn an ending (deus ex machina) except in deliberate antistructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting is four-dimensional
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting comprises period, duration, location, and level of conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design setting along these four axes and ensure setting choices support the story's causal logic and conflict level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study films like yours (break films down)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study films similar to your project; turn pages with the movie; break films down into setting, role, event, and value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exemplar films to learn rhythms, beats, scene types, and how comparable stories handle values and obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling Idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The controlling idea is the story’s ultimate meaning expressed through the action and aesthetic emotion of the last act’s climax; it has two components: value and cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatize the controlling idea in the climax without explanatory dialogue. The story's meaning must be shown via action and value change, not told.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist: requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A protagonist is willful, has a conscious desire (and possibly an unconscious one), has capacities to pursue the desire convincingly, and must have at least a chance to attain it; must be empathetic (not necessarily sympathetic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the protagonist has agency, credible capability, and a stake; hopeless protagonists with no chance of attainment cannot sustain audience interest. Unconscious desires can become the 'spine' and enrich complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience alignment and empathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences disassociate themselves from hypocrites; if a scene is emotionally meaningful to the writer it will likely be meaningful to the audience; humanity is conservative—people act when they must.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design character choices and arcs that create empathy, avoid hypocrisy, and present actions that feel necessary and believable to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three levels of conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict exists on three levels: extra-personal (society/world), personal (other characters), and inner (internal struggle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have conflict on all three levels. The quality of conflict should deepen across levels; use inner conflict to enrich character and outer conflict to raise stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character must make choices under pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: We learn who a character is through their choices under pressure; a character is defined by the choices they make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write scenes that force characters into dilemmas revealing true character; avoid self-explanatory dialogue—show through action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure desire by risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The measure of the value of a character’s desire is in direct proportion to the risk they are willing to take; greater value requires greater risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raise the stakes appropriately for the protagonist's desires; ensure willingness to risk demonstrates value and keeps audience investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write from the inside out / emotional truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Write from the inside out: find the center of a character and experience the story from their POV. The only source of emotional truth is the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate deep internal point-of-view; create scenes where inner life is expressed via objective, dramatized actions rather than exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Gap (action → reaction → gap)
rubrics_metrics.description: The substance of story is the gap between what a character expects to happen and what actually happens; action/reaction/gap — renewed action/surprising reaction/gap — builds great scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design scenes to open breaches between expectation and result; use opposite reactions to generate surprise and insight. Avoid scenes where reactions lack imagination (pace-killers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting Incident
rubrics_metrics.description: The inciting incident radically upsets the balance of forces in the protagonist’s life and must provoke a reaction; it creates an image of the climax in the audience’s mind and forms the 'spine' of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Execute the inciting incident as soon as the audience understands character and world; design it to jolt life into chaos and to point toward the climax. Consider how best/worst outcomes can invert expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive complications
rubrics_metrics.description: A story must move progressively forward toward a final action beyond which the audience cannot imagine another; nothing moves forward unless through conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase obstacles and complications steadily; avoid retreating to lesser actions. Ensure each complication deepens stakes or changes values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three major reversals minimum
rubrics_metrics.description: Three major reversals are the necessary minimum for a full-length narrative to reach 'the end of the line' (act structure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan at least three big reversals (typically aligned with act climaxes) to sustain progression toward the final climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act timing and key scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: The first act should be about 25% of the telling and the last act should be the shortest. A three-act story requires four memorable scenes: Inciting Incident, Act I, Act II, & Act III climaxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure pacing so setup takes about a quarter of runtime; ensure memorable climaxes at act transitions and keep final act compressed but intense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplot design and management
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot may contradict or resonate the controlling idea, enrich the film with irony or variation, or complicate the central plot; to deemphasize a subplot, keep crucial moments offscreen; parallel subplots that split the film equally will destroy focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subplots to deepen theme or contrast central plot; avoid equal-parallel subplots that divide audience attention; manage their inciting incidents, climaxes, and resolutions in relation to the main plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene design: turning points and unity
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene is a story in miniature, unified around desire, action, conflict, and change; each scene needs to be a minor, moderate, or major turning point and must cause a meaningful change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each scene has a clear desire, coherent action, opposition, and a value change; create turning points that deliver surprise, curiosity, insight, and new direction. Shape setups and payoffs carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setups and payoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Setups must be planted so they have one meaning initially and later take on a more important second meaning (payoff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plant set-ups visibly but subtly enough to be surprising at payoff; avoid setups so subtle they’re missed or so obvious they telegraph payoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion alternation & law of diminishing returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Story must create dynamic alternations from positive to negative emotions to obey the law of diminishing returns—repeated identical experiences lose impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary emotional valence and intensity to maintain impact. Space similar emotional beats and modulate magnitude to avoid audience fatigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful choices = dilemmas (triangular)
rubrics_metrics.description: True choice is dilemma—between two irreconcilable goods or the lesser of two evils; meaningful decisions are triangular (adding a third corner yields many variations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t stage obvious good/evil choices; design triangular dilemmas that force nuanced, revealing decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene analysis in five steps
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Define conflict (who/what drives the scene). 2) Note Opening Value (what value is at stake and its polarity). 3) Break the scene into beats (outer action vs subtextual action). 4) Note Closing Value and compare to opening. 5) Survey beats to locate the Turning Point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist to analyze or rewrite scenes; if value doesn't change, the scene is a nonevent. Adjust beats, desires, or actions to restore conflict and turn the scene properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition: unity and variety
rubrics_metrics.description: A story must be unified even when expressing chaos; unity is critical but must be accompanied by as much variety as possible (genre, tone, imagery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure a coherent controlling idea ties diverse scenes together; create variety (comic, dramatic, action elements) to enrich audience interest while maintaining thematic unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing, rhythm, and tempo (scene length guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm set by scene length; a typical 2‑hour feature has 40–60 scenes (~2½ minutes each). Tempo is activity level within scenes; progression of scenes should accelerate pace toward climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control scene length and internal tempo to shape rhythm. Alternate tension and relaxation; accelerate toward the climax while preserving profound change rather than mere speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressing progression (four techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four primary techniques to express progression: Social Progression (widen impact to society), Personal Progression (deepen intimate relationships/inner life), Symbolic Ascension (specific → universal imagery), Ironic Ascension (turn progression via irony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose one or more progression strategies to escalate stakes and thematic scope; align imagery and events to the chosen progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of transition (linking scenes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Find a third element that links scene A's tail to scene B's head—commonality or opposition: characterization, action, object, a repeated word, quality of light, a sound, or an idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transitions to create smooth narrative flow; look for symbolic or oppositional connectors rather than mechanical cuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis, Climax, Resolution requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis is the ultimate decision (true dilemma). Climax is a meaning-producing, absolute, irreversible value swing expressed by pure, clear action (no explanatory dialogue). Ending must be both inevitable and unexpected; resolution may be needed for subplots/support roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design crises as maximum-pressure dilemmas. Make climactic action self-evident and appropriate to the story. Provide tidy but honest resolutions for impacted supporting roles, but avoid artificial wrap-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of antagonism
rubrics_metrics.description: A protagonist and the story are only as compelling as the forces of antagonism; antagonism should make the protagonist an underdog with a chance but not a certainty of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build robust negative forces and chain reactions of antagonism that pay off naturally. Strong antagonism drives tragedy or comedy via negation patterns (negation of the negation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition: dramatize, don't tell
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition equals facts and must be dramatized to further conflict and convey necessary information; two characters shouldn’t tell each other things they both already know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert exposition into motivated dialogue or action (ammunition); parse exposition across the story; dramatize flashbacks as mini-dramas; test voice-over by removing it—if the story still works, keep it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems of interest: curiosity & concern (mystery, suspense, dramatic irony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Curiosity (audience knows less than characters), Suspense (audience and characters have same info), Dramatic Irony (audience knows more). These create engagement through mystery, suspense, or concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and sustain the appropriate interest mechanism; reward audience concentration with honest answers—avoid dirty tricks, false mysteries, or cheap surprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise: true vs cheap
rubrics_metrics.description: True surprise follows revelation of the gap between expectation and result and yields insight; cheap surprise exploits audience vulnerability (and is sometimes genre-conventional).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer true surprises that deepen meaning; cheap surprises can be used by genre convention (horror/thriller) but should be deployed knowingly and sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules about coincidence and deus ex machina
rubrics_metrics.description: Coincidence is an enemy unless given time to gain meaning; rule of thumb: do not use coincidence past the mid-point; never use coincidence to create an ending (deus ex machina) except in antistructure comedies/films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce coincidences early enough to make them meaningful; avoid 'god from the machine' endings which erase meaning and insult the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: anger & permitted devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is an angry, antisocial art; find what you are angry about and attack it. Comedy allows more coincidence and may allow deus ex machina if the protagonist has suffered and retained hope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base comedy on a clear, engaged anger/obsession; if using conventions (coincidence/deus ex), ensure audience sympathy through protagonist suffering and perseverance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation rules for medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Each medium has strengths: prose dramatizes inner conflict best, theater personal conflict, cinema extra-personal conflict. To adapt, read the source to feel its spirit, outline events succinctly, reorder chronologically, be willing to reinvent, express mental into physical, and stay within film rhythms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t slavishly copy source; cut, reorder, and invent visuals to express inner life. Read exemplars and create scene-by-scene outlines to compare. Avoid trying to adapt works centered on inner, linguistic complexity (e.g., Proust).

rubrics_metrics.name: Melodrama is under-motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Melodrama results from under-motivation (motivation doesn't match action), not overexpression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure actions are motivated by believable desires; avoid grand gestures that lack credible cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind Worm / character-specific inciting incident
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer should burrow into a character (mind-worm) to create an inciting incident tailored to their unique dreams, fears, strengths, and weaknesses that forces a one-of-a-kind quest revealing humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design inciting incidents that are uniquely suited to the protagonist’s psychology to maximize dramatic potential and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization vs true character; dimension = contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterization = observable qualities (appearance, mannerisms, speech). True character = moral/psychological core (loyal/ disloyal, honest/liar). Dimension comes from contradiction between facets (e.g., ambition vs guilt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build characters with consistent contradictions to create depth; avoid decorating with quirks alone. Ensure protagonist is the most dimensional character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cast design
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist creates the rest of the cast; polarization is key—roles should contrast or contradict; if two characters share attitude and react the same, collapse or expel one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design cast roles to dramatize and reflect protagonist contradictions; avoid making bit parts more interesting than necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three tips for writing screen characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave room for the actor; fall in love with all your characters; character is self-knowledge—ask 'If I were this character, what would I do?' and use honest answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write subtext and breathing room for actors, avoid writerly contempt of characters, and ground choices in the writer's honest imaginings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue: purpose, economy, and naturalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue is not mere conversation; it must say the maximum with the minimum words, have direction and purpose, turn beats, and sound like normal talk while being economical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim speeches (suspense sentence), favor subtext, avoid self-explanatory dialogue, and write dialogue late (after treatment) to avoid choking creativity. Prefer visual over verbal solutions when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description: write for the camera, use specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: A screenplay waits for the camera; most verbal expressions have no filmic equivalent. Use specific nouns and verbs, avoid 'is/are/there is' and 'we see/hear' constructions; write in present tense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer vivid, specific action lines ('he pads across the room' not 'he starts to slowly move'); delete nonfilmic constructions and transitions. Paint images that guide directors and actors without cinematic stage directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image systems (motifs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Image system — a strategy of motifs (category of imagery) that repeat in sight and sound with persistence and variation as subliminal communication to increase aesthetic emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design subliminal motif systems (objects, light, sound, animals, machines) and weave them consistently and subtly throughout the film to enrich meaning without calling attention to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title: name with meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: To title is to name; best titles often name two or all elements at once and hint at theme (e.g., Jaws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose titles that encapsulate character, setting, and theme succinctly; use a placeholder during development until a resonant title emerges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer's method: step outline → treatment → screenplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful writers start with a step-outline (one or two sentences per scene), then a treatment (expand scenes to paragraphs, no dialogue but subtext), then a screenplay (translate with dialogue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use step outlines to test viability quickly; expand into treatments and rework until every moment lives vividly before drafting dialogue. Be ruthless—trash what is weaker than your best work. Typical treatments vary in length; modern shorter 'treatments' may be inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of writing dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: The wise writer puts off writing dialogue as long as possible; premature dialogue can choke creativity and cause attachment to words over structural fixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop structure and subtext in treatment first; add dialogue later so fixes require structural revisions rather than line edits.
